Under Aaron Reese Boseman's direction, the outstanding cast brings to life the story of a house filled with two generations of free Black women and their enslaved servant that runs the gamut from harrowing to heartrending.
“That Will Not Stand” is not only a gripping drama with a stellar script, delicious design and standout performances—it will change how you view the legacy of human bondage.
Invictus answers with a production that is both eerie and elegant, steeped in laughter and lament.
Fortunately, the production is strong enough to withstand it.
As the title implies, the house itself is a character and a symbol of a history as tangled and ever-present as the Spanish moss that hangs over the roof
This production would certainly look perfectly comfortable on the Goodman, Steppenwolf or Shakespeare stages.
That Will Not Stand tells these women’s stories during a very specific time period and through powerful and striking performances.

Built with knowledge, passion, and dedication, director Aaron Reese Boseman delivers a show that powerfully centers Black female identity while confronting a dark, lesser-known chapter of American history.
The cast is powerful, and although the accents are often tough to understand, the story unfolds easily.

cn.t: Invictus Theatre's revival of Gardley's *The House That Will Not Stand* earns mostly strong notices for its powerful ensemble and rich exploration of race and misogyny in Creole New Orleans, with one dissenting voice finding the storytelling uneven.
